claim: Cognitive skills, not years of school attainment, are what relate to individual earnings, income distribution and economic growth
what_is_established_or_contested: established (review conclusion)
direction_or_sign: positive for skills; null/weak for attainment
reported_magnitude_verbatim: "It concludes that there is strong evidence that the cognitive skills of the population—rather than mere school attainment—are powerfully related to individual earnings, to the distribution of income, and to economic growth."
source_title: The Role of Cognitive Skills in Economic Development
notes: AEA article landing page opened; abstract read verbatim there. Full text paywalled.

claim: One standard deviation of student test performance is associated with roughly 1.2-2.0 percentage points per year faster GDP-per-capita growth
what_is_established_or_contested: established (association, cross-country panel); causal status contested
reported_magnitude_verbatim: "A move of one standard deviation of individual student performance translates into 1.2-2.0 percentage points difference in annual growth rates, other things equal."
source_title: Do better schools lead to more growth? Cognitive skills, economic outcomes, and causation
notes: Quote read in the IZA Discussion Paper No. 4575 (Nov 2009) version of the same paper, https://docs.iza.org/dp4575.pdf; the DP reports 1 SD = ~2 pp and a 1.2-2.0 pp range across specifications.

claim: With a direct cognitive-skill measure in the growth regression, years of school attainment lose statistical significance; explanatory power rises from about one-quarter to three-quarters of growth variance
what_is_established_or_contested: established (within these data/specifications)
direction_or_sign: null for attainment; positive for skills
reported_magnitude_verbatim: "School attainment is never statistically significant in the presence of the direct cognitive-skill measure of human capital." / "While this model explains one-quarter of the variance in growth rates, adding cognitive skills increases this to three-quarters of the variance."
source_title: Do better schools lead to more growth? Cognitive skills, economic outcomes, and causation
notes: Read in IZA DP 4575 text, Table 1 discussion. This is the clearest explicit 'years of schooling is a poor proxy' statement located in a mainstream macro paper.

claim: Causal identification of the skills-growth effect relies on instrumenting test scores with school-system institutions; IV estimates are close to OLS but the instrument is weak
what_is_established_or_contested: contested (identification)
reported_magnitude_verbatim: "the second stage of the instrumental variable (IV) estimation is statistically significant and close to the OLS estimate. However, the relatively low F-statistic of the instrument in the first stage indicates the possibility of a weak instrument problem."
source_title: Do better schools lead to more growth? Cognitive skills, economic outcomes, and causation
notes: Section V (instrumental variables) of IZA DP 4575. Authors' own hedging: 'suggest a causal interpretation', not proof.

claim: Book-length restatement: time in school is a misleading proxy for the skills that drive growth; results claimed robust across specifications, country subsets and causal tests
what_is_established_or_contested: established (authors' synthesis)
reported_magnitude_verbatim: "The common focus is on school attainment, although time in school provides a very misleading picture of how skills enter into development."
source_title: The Knowledge Capital of Nations: Education and the Economics of Growth
notes: RePEc/IDEAS book record opened; publisher description read. MIT Press page returned HTTP 403. Book text not accessed, so no book-level effect size claimed here.

claim: Three-quarters of cross-country variation in 1960-2000 growth of GDP per capita can be accounted for by international math and science test scores
what_is_established_or_contested: established (authors' summary of the research programme)
reported_magnitude_verbatim: "Over the period 1960–2000, three-quarters of the variation in growth of GDP per capita across countries can be accounted for by international measures of math and science skills."
source_title: Education and Economic Growth
venue: Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Economics and Finance (Oxford University Press)
notes: ABSTRACT READ FROM OPENALEX BIBLIOGRAPHIC RECORD (publisher URL returned 403/paywalled, not opened). Abstract text retrieved from the OpenAlex record for this DOI (abstract_inverted_index reconstituted); the OUP page itself was not opened and is paywalled. Treat as abstract-level verification only.

claim: Cross-national data show no association between the growth of educational capital and the growth rate of output per worker
what_is_established_or_contested: contested (the central negative result in the schooling-years literature)
direction_or_sign: null (growth of output per worker); implied negative association with TFP
reported_magnitude_verbatim: "Cross-national data show no association between increases in human capital attributable to the rising educational attainment of the labor force and the rate of growth of output per worker. This implies that the association of educational capital growth with conventional measures of total factor production is large, strongly statistically significant, and negative."
source_title: Where Has All the Education Gone?
notes: Published WBER version PDF (25 pp.) downloaded from the World Bank Documents & Reports server and read; page 367 abstract and Sections II-IV.

claim: Three candidate explanations for the shortfall: perverse governance, rapidly falling marginal returns to educated labour, and schooling quality so low that years create no human capital
what_is_established_or_contested: contested (interpretation of the null)
reported_magnitude_verbatim: "Third, educational quality could have been so low that years of schooling created no human capital."
source_title: Where Has All the Education Gone?
notes: Abstract, p.367. This is the direct textual ancestor of the later 'schooling ain't learning' argument.

claim: Growth-accounting logic implies the coefficient on educational capital should be roughly 0.21-0.42, i.e. about 0.3
what_is_established_or_contested: established (calibration benchmark, not an empirical estimate)
reported_magnitude_verbatim: "Hence the growth-accounting regression coefficient on educational capital (αh) ought to be between 0.21 and 0.42—with 0.3 in the middle of the range."
source_title: Where Has All the Education Gone?
notes: p.372-373, from the educational-capital-share-of-the-wage-bill calculation (Table 1). Useful as the 'what should we have expected' yardstick against which the null is judged.

claim: Book argument that schooling expansion has outrun learning: 'schooling is not the same as learning'; in rural Andhra Pradesh only about one in twenty fifth-graders could do basic arithmetic
what_is_established_or_contested: contested (diagnosis of a learning crisis)
reported_magnitude_verbatim: "In India's rural Andhra Pradesh, for instance, only about one in twenty children in fifth grade can perform basic arithmetic. The problem is that schooling is not the same as learning."
source_title: The Rebirth of Education: Schooling Ain't Learning
notes: Book has no DOI. This marketing/abstract text was seen only in a bibliographic record returned by the OpenAlex API; the CGD page and the book itself returned HTTP 403 and were NOT opened. Figure is a single Indian state illustration, not a cross-country estimate — do not generalise.

claim: Reconciling micro and macro: Mincerian private returns are strong, but the evidence that the stock of education raises a country's growth rate is tenuous and concentrated in very low-education countries
what_is_established_or_contested: contested (explicitly frames the macro return as fragile)
reported_magnitude_verbatim: "Our main conclusion is that while support for the micro Mincerian wage equation is strong, the evidence of a positive effect of the stock of education on a country's growth rate is tenuous."
source_title: Education for Growth: Why and For Whom?
notes: NBER Working Paper 7591 PDF (65 pp.) downloaded and read; quote from the paper's concluding section. Also states the positive initial-education effect 'applies primarily to countries with very low levels of education'.

claim: In a 98-country 1960-1985 cross-section, growth of real per capita GDP is positively related to initial human capital proxied by 1960 school-enrolment rates
what_is_established_or_contested: established (the baseline 'schooling matters' result in modern growth empirics)
reported_magnitude_verbatim: "For 98 countries in the period 1960–1985, the growth rate of real per capita GDP is positively related to initial human capital (proxied by 1960 school-enrollment rates) and negatively related to the initial (1960) level of real per capita GDP."
source_title: Economic Growth in a Cross Section of Countries
notes: ABSTRACT READ FROM OPENALEX BIBLIOGRAPHIC RECORD (publisher URL returned 403/paywalled, not opened). Abstract text retrieved from the OpenAlex record for this DOI (reconstituted from abstract_inverted_index); the OUP/JSTOR article page was not opened (paywall). Enrolment rates are a quantity proxy with no learning content — the point the skills literature later attacks.

claim: One extra year of male secondary-or-higher attainment raises the growth rate on impact by 0.44 pp; implied asymptotic output gain 19% and social return about 7%; female attainment insignificant; school quality quantitatively more important than quantity
what_is_established_or_contested: established (author's own estimates); contested vs. the skills literature on interpretation
direction_or_sign: positive but only for male secondary+; null for female and for primary
reported_magnitude_verbatim: "The estimated coefficient implies than an additional year of schooling (roughly a one-standard-deviation change) raises the growth rate on impact by 0.44% per year." / "the coefficient of 0.0044 on the schooling variable implies that an additional year of attainment for the typical adult raises the level of output asymptotically by 19%" / "the effect of school quality is quantitatively much more important"
source_title: Education and Economic Growth
notes: Full PDF (28 pp.) downloaded from the journal's own site and read. Note Barro still finds a significant years-of-schooling effect conditional on test scores — a genuine counterpoint to Hanushek-Woessmann's 'attainment insignificant' claim, though he agrees quality dominates.

claim: Extreme-bounds testing exaggerates fragility; analysing the full distribution of coefficients shows many variables are robustly related to growth
what_is_established_or_contested: contested (methodology of growth robustness)
direction_or_sign: methodological; supports robustness of some growth correlates
reported_magnitude_verbatim: "Instead, we find that a substantial number of variables can be found to be strongly related to growth."
source_title: I Just Ran Two Million Regressions
notes: ABSTRACT READ FROM OPENALEX BIBLIOGRAPHIC RECORD (publisher URL returned 403/paywalled, not opened). Abstract text retrieved from the OpenAlex record; full text not obtained (no open copy located; AEA and Columbia links returned 404). The paper's headline count of robust variables was NOT seen and is therefore not reported here.

claim: Better schooling data reverse the earlier null: with improved attainment series, schooling coefficients are significant in cross-country and panel growth regressions and the macro return matches labour studies
what_is_established_or_contested: contested (measurement error as the explanation for weak macro returns)
reported_magnitude_verbatim: "In standard cross-country growth regressions we find that our series yield significant coefficients for schooling. In panel data estimates our series are also significant even when the regressions account for the accumulation of physical capital. Moreover, the estimated macro return is consistent with those reported in labour studies. These results differ from the typical findings of the earlier literature and are a consequence of the reduction in measurement error in the series."
source_title: Growth and human capital: good data, good results
notes: RePEc/IDEAS article record opened and abstract read there. Springer page blocked. Important because it shows the schooling-vs-skills dispute is partly a data-construction dispute.

claim: Economic complexity (diversification/ubiquity eigenvector, ECI) is correlated with income per capita, and deviations of income from that relationship predict future growth
what_is_established_or_contested: established (founding claim of the field)
reported_magnitude_verbatim: "we show that the measures of complexity we derive are correlated with a country's level of income, and that deviations from this relationship are predictive of future growth."
source_title: The building blocks of economic complexity
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 106(26): 10570-10575
notes: PNAS site is Cloudflare-blocked; the full text was read from the authors' arXiv preprint arXiv:0909.3890 (https://arxiv.org/pdf/0909.3890), which is the same paper; the PNAS abstract was also read verbatim via the PMC record. Regression tables with R2 are in the Supplementary Material and were NOT seen — no magnitude is asserted here.

claim: The complexity measures outperform alternative measures of productive structure (Hirschman-Herfindahl concentration, entropy) in predicting growth
what_is_established_or_contested: established per authors; contested by later metric-comparison work
reported_magnitude_verbatim: "and that it is robust to the inclusion of other control variables such as individual country dummies (to capture any time-invariant country characteristic) and outperforms other indicators used to measure the productive structure of a country such as the Hirschman-Herfindahl [12,13] index and entropy measures [14]."
source_title: The building blocks of economic complexity
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 106(26): 10570-10575
notes: Read in arXiv:0909.3890 preprint, p.12. This is the closest thing in the founding paper to a 'beats export diversification' claim; the horse-race numbers sit in the unread SM.

claim: Product space is path dependent: a country's current export structure predicts which new products it can move into
what_is_established_or_contested: established (relatedness/path dependence is the field's most replicated result)
reported_magnitude_verbatim: "the evolution of Mcp exhibits strong path dependence, meaning that we can anticipate some properties a country's future new exports based on its current productive structure."
source_title: The building blocks of economic complexity
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 106(26): 10570-10575
notes: Read in arXiv:0909.3890, p.12-13. Relevant to massification because it implies skill formation is constrained by existing industrial structure.

claim: Measurement caveat acknowledged inside the field: EXPY-style sophistication measures are built with GDP-per-capita weights, whereas ECI uses only country-product links
what_is_established_or_contested: contested (what the index actually measures)
reported_magnitude_verbatim: "However, this paper uses information on GDP per capita to calculate export sophistication, while Hidalgo and Hausmann (2009) use only the links between countries and products. This implies that the result depends on the structure of the network and not on the GDP measures."
source_title: The network structure of economic output
notes: Read in arXiv:1101.1707 preprint, footnote 2. Useful because it admits that a widely used complexity/sophistication measure embeds income by construction.

claim: A simpler export-based complexity metric (ECI+) predicts growth better than both ECI and Fitness-complexity; one SD of ECI+ corresponds to about 4-5% faster annualized growth
what_is_established_or_contested: contested (which metric to use; not peer reviewed)
reported_magnitude_verbatim: "We find that ECI+ outperforms ECI and Fitness in its ability to predict economic growth and in the consistency of its estimators across most econometric specifications. On average, one standard deviation increase in ECI+ is associated with an increase in annualized growth of about 4% to 5%."
source_authors: Albeaik, Saleh; Kaltenberg, Mary; Alsaleh, Mansour; Hidalgo, Cesar A.
source_title: Improving the Economic Complexity Index
notes: 21-page preprint downloaded and read. NOT peer reviewed — do not cite as if journal-published. Its own framing concedes that the choice of complexity metric changes the growth coefficient, which is the key fragility.

claim: ECI+ and the original ECI are correlated at R-squared of about 85% but rank countries differently, especially manufacturing-heavy exporters
what_is_established_or_contested: contested (metrics agree on average, disagree in ranking)
reported_magnitude_verbatim: "ECI+ and ECI have a strong correlation (R2=85%), but ECI+ tends to rank manufacturing heavy countries higher than ECI (ECI+ ranks Vietnam higher than Qatar and China higher than"
source_authors: Albeaik, Saleh; Kaltenberg, Mary; Alsaleh, Mansour; Hidalgo, Cesar A.
source_title: Improving the Economic Complexity Index
notes: p.9 of the preprint; quote ends mid-sentence in the extracted text (line break), verbatim as seen.

claim: The ECI is mathematically equivalent to a spectral clustering / dimension-reduction algorithm on a country-similarity graph, not a direct measure of latent capabilities
what_is_established_or_contested: contested (construct validity / mechanism)
reported_magnitude_verbatim: "We show that the ECI is, in fact, equivalent to a spectral clustering algorithm, which partitions a similarity graph into two parts."
source_authors: Mealy, Penny; Farmer, J. Doyne; Teytelboym, Alexander
source_title: A New Interpretation of the Economic Complexity Index
notes: Working paper dated 4 February 2018, downloaded and read. This is the sharpest 'the mechanism is disputed' citation: if ECI is a clustering device, 'productive knowledge' is an interpretation, not an identified quantity. Check whether a peer-reviewed version exists before citing in print.

claim: The commonly used complexity methodologies produce contrasting country rankings, which undermines their acceptance and application
what_is_established_or_contested: contested (metric disagreement)
reported_magnitude_verbatim: "The commonly used methodologies to measure economic complexity produce contrasting results, undermining their acceptance and applications."
source_authors: Sciarra, Carla; Chiarotti, Guido; Ridolfi, Luca; Laio, Francesco
source_title: Reconciling contrasting views on economic complexity
notes: Open-access PDF downloaded and read. Authors argue the disagreement is reconcilable via linear algebra, but the disagreement itself is the documented fact.

claim: ECI is a significant negative predictor of income inequality, and predicts inequality better than income per capita does
what_is_established_or_contested: established per authors (replicated association); mechanism disputed
reported_magnitude_verbatim: "the negative relationship between economic complexity and income inequality (R2=0.58, p-value=~10-16) is stronger than the relationship between income inequality and GDP per capita (R2=0.36, p-value= ~10-10)" ; table cell "ECI -0.040***"
source_authors: Hartmann, Dominik; Guevara, Miguel R.; Jara-Figueroa, Cristian; Aristaran, Manuel; Hidalgo, Cesar A.
source_title: Linking Economic Complexity, Institutions, and Income Inequality
notes: Numbers read in arXiv:1505.07907 draft (Sept 2016). The -0.040 coefficient is from a multivariate Gini regression with income, schooling, rule of law, corruption control and population controls (table, p.~20 of draft).

claim: Trade-based complexity adds explanatory power to a convergence baseline for 10-year growth, and multidimensional (trade+technology) complexity adds about 7 more points of adjusted R-squared
what_is_established_or_contested: established per authors (out-of-sample-ish panel fit); magnitude depends on metric set
reported_magnitude_verbatim: "This captures Solow's idea of economic convergence (the baseline model is presented in column 1 of Table 1, adjusted R2 ¼ 0:25). ... We find that trade complexity is a significant and positive predictor of economic growth (column 2, adjusted R2 ¼ 0:34) ... The multidimensional model leads to an improvement in explanatory power over the trade complexity regression of 7 percentage points (adjusted R2 ¼ 0:41)."
source_authors: Stojkoski, Viktor; Koch, Philipp; Hidalgo, Cesar A.
source_title: Multidimensional economic complexity and inclusive green growth
notes: Open-access PDF downloaded and read. Verbatim text contains PDF-ligature artefacts (¼ for =); numbers are 0.25, 0.34, 0.41. Best modern statement of 'how much does ECI add beyond income convergence'.

claim: Review: economic complexity metrics explain and predict international and regional variation in income, growth, inequality and emissions, and relatedness measures anticipate changes in specialisation
what_is_established_or_contested: established (review-level synthesis); the review is by a field founder
reported_magnitude_verbatim: "Measures of economic complexity explain and predict international and regional variations in income, economic growth, income inequality, gender inequality and greenhouse emissions."
source_title: Economic complexity theory and applications
notes: Landing page opened; only abstract, key points and reference list were readable (article body paywalled). No effect size visible on the page, so none is reported.

claim: The Growth Lab / Atlas institutionalises ECI as a forecasting and ranking instrument (annual country complexity ranking and growth projections)
what_is_established_or_contested: established (institutional practice); no causal claim implied
reported_magnitude_verbatim: "Discover the countries rising and falling in Harvard Growth Lab's annual country growth projections." / "Explore Harvard Growth Lab's annual ranking of country and product complexity."
source_authors: Hausmann, Ricardo; Hidalgo, Cesar A.; et al. (Growth Lab)
source_title: The Atlas of Economic Complexity: Mapping Paths to Prosperity
venue: MIT Press; online at Harvard Growth Lab Atlas
notes: Atlas web platform opened (JavaScript app; only descriptive text readable). The 2014 book PDF could not be fully downloaded (truncated transfer) and the MIT Press page returned HTTP 403 — so no book-level magnitude is claimed. Verified only that the Atlas/Growth Lab publicly ranks countries by ECI and publishes growth projections.

claim: Alternative operationalisation: classify 779 products by sophistication and connectivity rather than by ECI, yielding 'good'/'bad' products and several 'product traps'
what_is_established_or_contested: contested (which structural measure matters; different taxonomy, no growth regression)
reported_magnitude_verbatim: "We identify 352 "good" products and 427 "bad" products. ... We find 28 countries in a "middle product" trap."
source_authors: Felipe, Jesus; Kumar, Utsav; Abdon, Arnelyn
source_title: How Rich Countries Became Rich and Why Poor Countries Remain Poor: It's the Economic Structure... Duh!
venue: Levy Economics Institute Working Paper No. 644
notes: 55-page working paper downloaded and read. NOTE: this paper contains no growth regression and does not directly test ECI's predictive power; cite it for the alternative taxonomy and the 'structure matters' argument, not as an ECI refutation.
